name: Achaemenid Empire

fields.foundation: The Achaemenid Empire, the first Persian Empire, was founded by Cyrus II (Cyrus the Great) after he became King of Anshan in Persia around 559 BCE. At that point the Persian kingdom was a minor vassal of the Median Empire under Astyages; within thirty years it would become the largest empire the world had yet seen. Cyrus revolted against Astyages and defeated him in 550 BCE, when the Median army mutinied and surrendered its king. A single campaign thus gave Cyrus the Median territories, from the Iranian plateau to eastern Anatolia as far as the Halys river. He then defeated Croesus of Lydia, traditionally at the Battle of Thymbra, and captured Sardis around 547–546 BCE, bringing the Ionian Greek cities of the Aegean coast under Persian suzerainty. In 539 BCE Cyrus defeated the Babylonian army at the Battle of Opis and entered Babylon, absorbing the Neo-Babylonian Empire with little resistance. The Cyrus Cylinder, issued after the conquest, permitted deported peoples to return to their homelands and sanctioned the restoration of temples, and it is often celebrated as one of history's earliest statements of religious tolerance. Cyrus thus set the pattern of Achaemenid rule, which legitimised conquest by taking over the existing political and religious traditions of the conquered. His son Cambyses II defeated Pharaoh Psamtik III at the Battle of Pelusium in 525 BCE and incorporated Egypt, where the Persian kings count as its 27th Dynasty. Achaemenid authority now reached across three continents.
fields.socioeconomy: The Achaemenid Empire ruled a large proportion of the world's population (modern estimates vary widely) and drew revenues from the most productive agricultural regions of the ancient world: Mesopotamia, Egypt and the Levant. Darius I (r. 522–486 BCE) formalised the economic administration by dividing the empire into satrapies, twenty according to Herodotus, each assessed a fixed annual tribute. The gold daric and silver siglos gave a common royal coinage to an empire that reached from the Indus to the Aegean. The Royal Road ran some 2,700 kilometres from Susa to Sardis. Relays of royal couriers could cover the distance in around a week, and goods, armies and officials moved along it across the imperial heartland. Trade networks connected Persia to the Indian subcontinent, Central Asia and the Mediterranean, and a canal completed under Darius linked the Nile to the Red Sea. The Achaemenid kings tolerated local customs, languages and religious practices to a high degree, a deliberate policy that reduced the cost of governing diverse subject populations. Local elites were co-opted into the administration, Persian garrisons kept order without displacing indigenous social structures, and royal inscriptions were produced in several languages. Egypt's grain surplus and Babylon's commercial revenues mattered most to the treasury, and the loss of Egypt for six decades after 404 BCE was the most damaging single economic blow the empire sustained before its final collapse.
fields.military: At its height the Achaemenid military could put armies in the field on three continents. Its core was the Persian infantry and cavalry, supplemented by contingents from every subject nation, including Medes, Babylonians, Egyptians, Lydians and Indians, which made it the most ethnically diverse army the ancient world had seen. After suppressing the great revolts of 522–520 BCE that followed his accession, Darius I reorganised it into a more professional and systematically ordered force. The Immortals were the empire's elite infantry, a corps which, according to Herodotus, was always kept at exactly ten thousand men. Its campaigns included Cyrus's conquest of Lydia, where camels were reportedly deployed to unsettle the Lydian cavalry, the conquest of Egypt (525 BCE), Darius's Scythian campaign (c. 513 BCE), and Xerxes's massive invasion of Greece (480 BCE), which brought victory at Thermopylae and the sack of Athens. The Greek Wars showed the limits of Persian arms against determined Greek hoplites and fleets, at Marathon (490 BCE), Salamis (480 BCE) and Plataea (479 BCE). From the Persian perspective, however, the failure to subjugate Greece was a peripheral setback that left the empire's Asian and African heartland untouched. The decisive military collapse came only with Alexander the Great's campaigns (334–330 BCE), when a tactically superior Macedonian army defeated Persian forces at the Granicus, Issus and Gaugamela in rapid succession.
fields.governance: The Achaemenid administrative system, as elaborated by Darius I, was the most developed the ancient world had yet produced. The empire was divided into provinces, each governed by a satrap, typically a Persian nobleman and often a relative of the royal house. He held civil and judicial authority within his territory, while separate officials commanded the chief garrisons. Royal agents, known in Greek sources as the "Eyes and Ears of the King", reported on the conduct of the satraps directly to the monarch, which made it harder for a satrap to entrench himself as an independent ruler. The Royal Road's courier system let the king communicate with the furthest corners of the empire within days, and Imperial Aramaic was the administrative lingua franca across the satrapies whatever the local language. Persepolis was the ceremonial capital where the empire's subject nations presented tribute, Susa the principal administrative centre and Ecbatana the summer residence. Darius promoted a royal law that drew on existing Babylonian, Egyptian and Persian legal traditions and gave a degree of uniformity without eliminating local customary law. This tolerance for local institutions was a deliberate strategy: Cyrus framed the conquest of Babylon as the restoration of Marduk's favour, and the Achaemenid kings consistently sought legitimacy within the religious frameworks of their subjects, ruling as pharaoh in Egypt and as restorer of religious order in Babylonia.
fields.impact: The effects of Achaemenid rule on the politics and culture of the ancient world long outlasted the empire. It governed a territory stretching from the Indus to the Aegean and from Central Asia to the Nile, the largest multi-ethnic political order yet seen, and established the precedent of a universal empire that crossed ethnic and linguistic boundaries. The administrative innovations of Darius I, including the satrapal system, the Royal Road, royal coinage and the use of Aramaic as an administrative language, influenced every subsequent empire of the ancient Near East, including the Seleucid, Parthian and Sasanian states that successively governed the Iranian plateau. Alexander the Great consciously adopted the Achaemenid model of religious tolerance and administrative decentralisation, and presented himself as the legitimate heir to Achaemenid authority in Persia, Egypt and Babylon rather than simply as a conqueror. By bringing Greek, Egyptian, Babylonian and Indian traditions into a single political space the empire prepared the ground for the Hellenistic synthesis that followed. The Cyrus Cylinder has been celebrated in modern times as an early articulation of humane rule, and the Achaemenid treatment of the Jewish exiles in Babylonia, allowing the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem, had lasting consequences for the development of Judaism.
fields.decline: The Achaemenid Empire eroded gradually and then collapsed suddenly. The erosion began not with the Greek Wars, a peripheral embarrassment from the Persian perspective, but with the loss of Egypt in 404 BCE, when the province revolted successfully at the death of Darius II and remained independent under native dynasties for some six decades until Artaxerxes III reconquered it in 343 BCE. In the Revolt of Cyrus the Younger (401 BCE) a Persian prince hired Greek mercenaries to contest the throne and died at Cunaxa. The strategic damage was especially great: Xenophon's Anabasis showed that a relatively small Greek force could march through the Persian heartland and escape, and so that the empire was vulnerable to any sufficiently determined adversary. The Great Satraps' Revolt (c. 372–362 BCE) showed that the satrapal system itself had become a source of fragmentation. The poisoning of the capable Artaxerxes III in 338 BCE by the court eunuch Bagoas removed the last ruler capable of renewing its institutions and left the empire weakened before Alexander crossed the Hellespont. The final collapse (334–330 BCE) was unusually rapid for an empire of more than two centuries: Alexander defeated Persian forces at the Granicus (334 BCE), Issus (333 BCE) and Gaugamela (331 BCE), occupied Persepolis and burned its palaces in 330 BCE, and Darius III was murdered by his own satrap Bessus that summer.
fields.summary: The Achaemenid Empire shows how the administrative ability of individual rulers, above all Cyrus and Darius, can create a durable structure, and how the loss of capable central leadership can bring that structure down within a generation. It was the first great multi-ethnic administrative state, tolerant of local religion, language and custom while imposing a unifying imperial framework, and later world powers, consciously or not, would follow its template of empire.
fields.teaser: Founded by Cyrus the Great, the Achaemenid Persian Empire was the largest the world had yet seen, stretching from the Balkans and Egypt to the Indus. It was known for tolerating the religions and customs of its subject peoples.
fields.t0: The first Persian Empire, built by Cyrus the Great, stretched from the Indus to the Aegean and the Nile.
fields.t1: Darius I's satrapies, Royal Road, coinage and Aramaic chancery became the model for later Near Eastern empires.
fields.t2: Weakened by revolts and court murders, it fell to Alexander the Great in just four years, 334 to 330 BCE.
fields.dyk: Royal couriers on the 2,700-kilometre Royal Road from Susa to Sardis could cover the distance in around a week, using relays of fresh riders.
